div.head: WARRINGTON CONTINGENT FOR THE KING'S REVIEW. (Photographed at Bank Quay Station on their return on Wednesday.)
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CONTINGENT FOR THE KING'S REVIEW. (Photographed at Bank Quay Station on their return on Wednesday.)

Warrington and Widnes contributed 59 wont. masters and boos to the great King's rally at Windsor on Tuesday. 'they aasembled at Howard's Place at 115)) on Monday night when Major Appleton addrestad a few words to them, giving some good advice and impressing upon them the import .nce of loyalty ri their King and country and our great Empire. The bvs were then marched to Rank Quay Static n edere Ihey were met by Mr. Fulton-Sinith and provided with hot coffee, cocoa and meat pies. The train was compomd of corridor carriages winch were niust comfortable and convenient for a long journey and the greatest credit is due to the L. A N -W. Railway fur this consideration. At Willesden Junction the train was handed ivar to the L. A S.-W. Railway and Windsor nag reached about 7 am. The baggage havit g been handed over to the A.S.C., the bops were marched to their Assembly , Ground via Alma-road. This was the east side 'I the Long Walk and ilet north of the camping ground. The boys were ordered to re-assemble at 11 .Silent, and during the interval refreshed themselves with mineral water and cakes. They were also greatly interested in the I:el:Jars' camp which con- sisted of Dragoon Guards, A.S.C. and A O.C. detach- ments. The Canadian and Australian Scours, tegether with those from Gibraltar came in for great attention.

At 1 o'clock the first grin was fircd, and the boys took up their places in de e ectir n allotted to theta, which was 13 and 14 Troops, Section It, Itivision VI. Another gun was fir td at 1.30 and the boys seers prepartd for taking up their Oace in the semi-circle on the Review Ground. This was a great movement, and consisted of each section of 1,210 boys marching in one body close column of Troops 21 nu each troop. The orderly manner in which this was carried out would have dote an.ple credit to the loot-rained Ilenulars. A third gnu was fired at 2 o'clock, which denoted that all were t, be in their exact position for

the Royal Review. About '2.30 went up the grratest cheer, which the world has ever heard, for there is no cheer like that of a Itoy Scout, which is given with sincerity and fullness I heart. The idol of the Boy Scouts (liners! Baden Powell was ridirg throuk,h the lines inspecting the arrangement of the divisions ewtior.s and troops lint he had no Amendments to add for everything had been cart led cut to the letter and mint tin . roughlv -„ • • .•

At 2.50 the' Queen, Prinerss Christian, Princess Mary- and the Prince of Wales drove on the ground and came in for a good round of cheering flora the 6,000 spectators assembled in the enclosures and on stands. Punctually at 3 o'clock the King accompanied by Prince Christian, the Duke of Com.aught, Lord Roberts, Lord Grenfell, Indian Pointe, and with an escort of Life Guards mounted on fine chargers, rode on the ground. 1 here were tin gaudy uniforms, the whole of the cavalcade being attired in simple undrape uniforms. Evety boy was afforded the privilege of seeing the Kirg twice at close quarters, for after he passed along the front cf a semi-circle the b ye were i• turned about and tine rear became the front so that I they also had a full new of his 31ajesty. The Queen. Prince Chi istiaa, Princess Mary, and Pt ince of Wales seated in a landau,hol lowed the King through the tab le of the inspection. Duo ing the inspection some of the patrols gave exhibitions of parade fire lighting and first aid. Whilst the King's Scouts and Life Guards marched past the King tine who!rs of the in .ya led by the magnificent band rf the Coldstream threats, sang the Scotia' song, " Boys' be prepared," by Rubeas. The rally. which was the most wonder ful part of the whole proceedings, came nest. At a signal from the General a seething mass of 35,000 ran in for NO yards towards one counnon centre, cheering and calling their patrol calls. 'three cheers for the King were called for, up went a forest of staves, each nine' Imounted by • scout', hat, and three of the mo,t lusty cheers ever given came from a nuiloitude of throats.

The National Anthem was played and song. and the King tal I. ii dr Failure amid demonstrations of loyalty .11 along the I heard the remark passed by many tluit Windmr bad been the place for wonderful reviews. hut there had recur Igen one t, equal that of the Boy Scouts. Windsor was given over to the Boy Scouts for the •Imle of the evening and it was no uric mmon sight to see a sin to t guardsman tresting a Lumber of Boy Scoots ti a sail on the Thames. The inhabitants and visitors in Winds,were moat courtehns end kind to every Scout, and one officer of the Coldstream Gualds invited a band of about Si Scoutmasters whom he had met looking round the barracks. to luncheon.

The tal'y completed, tie boys from Warrington and Widnes were marched into cat..pwnel tints ahcrted to them. A plentiful supply of warm blankets, with oil shot ts, was obtained from the A S.C. Stores, and the buys laid out their beds ready fore well-earned rest. Tea was partaken of and the boys dispersed to find enjoyment, some going around the Castle, some for a mil and others for a stroll around the beautiful great park with its herds if deer.
„ The boye were op at 53,, the feline ing mnrnieg, and an cpen•air beth in the Thames was greatly enjoyed by many. . _

rl Ile kitbags were placed on Transport Waggons at 9 a in. and the boys paraded at 131) and marched to the btation. Punctually at 10 30 the train started for the north. Ilefrebhmects were obtained at Northampton, nod W•rringtou was reached at 13lpm. The troops marched along SJukey-strek and Buttermarket-street to !Towards Place led by the Bugle Band if the fit Warrington Troop. Cheers were given for the King end the troops dispersed. Thus ended the moot memorable event iu the life cf the donut up to the present time. .

div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONS.
DIOCESAN FESTIVAL AT WARRINGTON
A Colonel's Tribute to Missionary Work.

Thursday witnessed ii unique event, as far 89 Wartington is concerned, the Liverpool Diocesan Board of Missions holding its annual featival in this toes. An interesting levies of services and meetings took place and, notwithstanding the beautiful summer weather. there were good attendances. At 7.3.) um. the Holy Communion was celebrated at the Parish Church and other churchee, special pet,tions being offered on behalf of missionary work. At noon a serv;ce was held in the Pariah Church, the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) conducting the special form of intercession and thanks• giving drawn up by the Foreign Missions Committee of the London Itioce,an Conference. The preacher was the Rev. J 0 F. Murray, DD.. Master of Selwyn College. Cambridge. who based an earnest and power- fill discourse on the word, " Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word That they all may be one ; as thou Father, art in me. and I in thee, that they also may be one in its ; that the world may believe that thou has soot me. And the glory which thou gayest me. I have given them ; that they rosy be one as we are one." (St. John xvii.. Ile said the more he thought upon the subject the more he felt ruin aced that the deepest, moist far- ratching, and most indispensable part of the work which was given to Church peop'e at home on behalf of miesionary work abroad was that of intercession. The preacher impressed upon his hearers the der th of the unity which Christ prayed for on behalf of His followers. It was not tube merely a itnity from with- out external, inechanicaLor by compulsion. What lle wan longing for was a unity of a different kind—a unity that was vital, organic, from within The only perfect expression which we could put before our minds as we prayed won the units of the Father and the Son, that unity of perfect mutual love. unselfishness and subordination the one to the ether. That was the goal which the Lord put before us. When that goal was reached, external and s isible union could n 4 t be far away. It moot Come to express before area that which was the 10W3rd and abiding fret. The preacher urgt d his bearers to pray for Lindy at home and abroad, knowicg that on it ultimately depended the fulfilment of their great mission to being all the nation, into obediente to the will of God and of our &vicar Jesus Christ.

Man is the only animal that walks up- right; the muscles of his bark and the liga- ments that bind the bones of th.• spine I•i- -g,ther are put to an enormous strain IA maintaining the erect position. div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Ptlllp Snowden, N P
_ SOME DIFFICULTIES IN THE INSUR- ANCE BILL. HOW IT WILL AFFECT

div.head: TRADE UNIONS.
div.p: TRADE UNIONS.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer will take a course which is all but universally con- demned if he tries to force the Insurance Bill ' through the House of Commons by the means of the guillotine. This is not a party measure. All sections profess to be anxious only to make the Bill as practical and work- able as possible. The Chancellor can only get the Bill passed by one of two ways. He can, as he has proposed, use the party whips to force men into the division lobbies against their wills to vote for the Government, or he can allow the House of Commons ample time to mould it into a scheme which will be satisfactory to the great majority. There never was a moasure brought into Parliament so full of intricate and complex difficulties. The more one examines the Bill and the more one is forced to the conclusion that it would be a disaster to allow the scheme to come into operation in its present immature and unshaped form. The Chancellor, according to his own statement, has been spending his days and nights upon this bill for three years, with the assistance of the most able advisers he could obtain, and yet he expects the country to take it with a few weeks consideration, practically denying the House of Commons the right to make any amendment. The two hours' catechism which the Chancellor underwent at the hands of the Friendly Societies (lid not after all make the position very much clearer. A large num- ber of points are still left in doubt and obscurity. Indeed the answers to some of the questions raised new difficulties. The reply upon the point about admittingeollect- ing friendly societies and insurance companies " approved societies" tinder the Bill appears to convey the suggestion that any kind of an organisation of sufficient numbers can qualify for approval. This seems very much like a breach of the original bargain with the friendly societies, and it is no doubt due to the influence which the insurance companies have brought to bear upon the Chancellor. Without arguing the question at all it may be painted out that if every kind of a society with 5,000 members (the number he is now prepared to make the minimum) is to be recognised, the friendly societies are going to have to face a formid- able competition from collecting societies, dividing societies, insurance companies, and , business firms like railway companies, great engineering firms, and the like employing large numbers of workmen.

div.head: TRADE UNIONS AS "APPROVED SOCIETIES."
div.p: TRADE UNIONS AS "APPROVED SOCIETIES."

The trade unions will stand a very poor chance of becoming "approved societies" under the Bill. At present they are not able to qualify, but the Chancellor has said that It is his intention that they should be snowed to do so, and, if necessary, amend- ments will be inserted to make that possible. But there are comparatively very few trade unions in this country whose membership exceeds 5,000, and it must be pointed out that the membership will not be the member- ship of the union for trade union purposes but only such as elect to make their trade union their approved society for the purposes of this Ac'. In many of the great trade unions the percentage of members who contribute for friendly benefits is only a very small proportion of the total. In the Railway way Men's Union, for instance, it is only about 4 per cent. There are no figures on the point, but I should say that the vast majority, probably 90 per cent, of the membership of the trade unions are also members of friendly societies l'hey will be able to choose whether they will select the trade union or the friendly society as the approved society. The trade unions which desire to qualify as app-oved socioties will have to separate their funds. mond they will therefore be faced with this mdifficulty. If they set aside any considerable portion of their funds as a reserve for friendly society benefits they will be dining the fighting fund of .he union. If they do not do that they will have a difficulty in satisfy- ing the financial requirements of an "approved society," and they will not be able to give the additional benefits which a good frierdly society can give.

div.head: MATTER OF CHOICE.
div.p: A MATTER OF CHOICE.

The member of a trade union who is also a member of a good friendly society will have to decide whether he will put his trade unionism before his friendly society, which in the majority of cases will mean that he will sacrifice a good deal in the way of benefits. It is estimated in the scheme that there will be on the average 10 per cent margin avail- able for additional benefits. The well managed societies, and those with large reserve funds, will have much more than this, and therefore it will be to the financial interest of the insured workman to select the society which promises to give him the best return, and in this respect the trade unions will be at a decided disadvantage. Trade unions may suffer in another way from the effects of this Insurance Scheme. One of the reasons why some men join a trade union is because it gives out of work pay and superannuation. When the work- man can get these through a National Insurance Scheme one of the inducements to join a trade union will be removed. In another way, too, the effect upon the trade unions is likely to be serious. There is a bottom to the pocket of the workingman. He cannot go on paying something for this and some- thing for that without being forced to cut off his expenditure in other directions. It is a difficult enough thing at present to get the few coppers a week from the low wage of the unskilled workman as a contribution to a trade union. These are the men who to a great extent are not members of friendly societies, or rather they are the men who join and fall out to the extent of 250,000 a year. They simply cannot afford to pay. Under this Insurance Scheme they will have to pay. When they are in work they will have the 4d. a week deducted from their wages, and they will therefore turn round to see how they can economise in another direction. It is likely that in many cases it will be the trade union contribution which will suffer. ANOTHER SERIOUS POINT.

The trade unions are not unlikely to suffer in another way. As has been pointed out, if thc Bill is amended as promised so that a trade union fulfilling the necessary conditions can qualify as an approved society, any trade union becoming an approved society will be required to separate its funds, and under ' penalties, will not be allowed to use the insurance contributions for other purposes. At present every trade union, if it needs money. uses all its accumulated funds for strike purposes, but that will not be possible if it becomes an "approved society." The

fighting power of the trade union will thereby be greatly reduced. These are just a few, and only a very few points arising on the consideration of this Insurance Bill as it is likely to affect organised labour. From that point of view the Bill requires the most serious considera- tion of trade unionists. It did not receive! that consideration at the Conference recently' held in London. That Conference seemed happily unconscious of the serious way in which the trade unions would be affected by the Bill if it passed in anything like its present form. I think the Conference made a great mistake, not only from the point of view of the interests of trade unionism, but from the point of view of the welfare of the workers 03 a class in giving its approval to the principle of contributions from the work- men. This is bad in principle, it is opposed to all the tendencies of recent social reform ; it puts a burden on the workers they cannot and ought not to bear; and it creates enormous difficulties ab mt administration which would be avoided if the same principle and practice we have in the Old Age Pensions Act, the Workmen's Compensation Act, the Education Act, and the like, had been applied tu the Insurance of workers against Sickness and Unemployment.

On all sides of mil se I vor:te there are fields upon fields containing large qnsrititie.s of hay that have suffered severely OA ing to the heavy nrin of the last two or three weeks. An inch of rainfsll represents 100 tons of water to the act'. Just think of it ! Statistic .1 friends might make it the basis of an elabor- ate calculation. I was writing of the hay-fields where the frequent showers have In • few rdnutes quite undone or prevented what otherwise the good stiff breezes and such sultana° as has kupervened might , Inve effected, whereas these hare in not a few cases really done more harm than good. I remmtber h in a former uncongenial and wet season, and agricul- tural correspondent pointed out that in Norway, where sea one are, ass rule, worse for the hay than is this c !retry, roughly-built wire or wooden fences are always in readiness, and nver Vies% the hay-grass is flung, I, unable the breeze to expedite the drying. and also to prevent the c.op becoming so saturated, as when spread on the ground. In Scotland the grass is often thrown across the walls. The free admixture of salt with injured hay, at the time it is being stacked or housed, is one of the best means of restor- ing quality, but, of course, it adds to the expense It is difficult for dwellers in these parts to conceive of countries where rain is the exception, not the rule. A week ago it was remarked in this paper that orematioo still makes but slow progress. 'the 1t... C. Let me quote from a , Cremation Society pamphlet. "Whew it is considered " observes the writer, " that about 72,000 persons ' die in London every year—or NO a day—it is almost incredible that people will go on wowing the ground around the city in which they live with a ring of decomposing matter, when by means of cremation a human body can be reduced in the space of an h into harmless gases and a small amount of clean white ash.'"the latter, I suppose, would merely weigh half-a-dozen ounces or It is further urged by the advocates of cremation that it is more sanitary than pit burial ; it is cheaper—and would be much more so if more generally adopted ; it interf reit with no religious ceremony or rite ; it admits of the same ceremonial an if ordinary burial were resorted to ; it spares friends the discomfort and danger, especially in inclement weather, of attending a graveside. thus obviating one of the newt distreasing features if burial; it has been recognised by l'arliatueut, which has Unmet] stringent regulation. on the aubject ; it removes the Powsiblliq of any one being buried alive; and it is a much more effective safeguard against foul play than in he NH" of ordinary burial —the death to, titration required being far stricter Then there is the aesthetic or sentimental side of the question. A FLORAL CLOCK.

It would be possible if one bad the time ' and patience to make a floral clock, that is to say to arrange a row of flowers and be able to tell the time by looking at them. The reaFon why this is possible is because the flowers are most regular and accurate in their time of opening and shutting. Let me tell you how the clock could be made. The yellow goats beard comes first, it opens at three in the morning, the blue wild Ichichory at four, the yellow common nipplewort at five, the golden butter- cup at six, the white waterlily at

seven, the scarlet pimpernel at eighjt, the golden lesser celandine at nine. The common nipplewort closes at ten, the white common star of Bethlehem opens at eleven, the yellow goatsbeard closes at noon, the proliferous pink closes at one p.m., the scarlet pimpernel closes at two, the yellow rough dandelion at three, the wild chicory at four, the white waterlily at five. The white Nottingham catchfly opens at six, the yellow evening primrose at seven. Unless there happens to be a pond near, it would be rather difficult to have the waterlily, but the other flowers could be very easily grown. I do not know whether such a clock has ever been made but I am sure it is possible and if the flowers were placed in a circle the effect would be very interesting.

div.head: HEROIC DOGS.
div.p: HEROIC DOGS.
I In France the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals decorates dogs who have distinguished themselves by deeds of bravery, with a collar tastefully designed, called "Collar of Honour."

Among the animals decorated in this way, one of the most celebrated is Bacchus, a large bulldog, whose speciality it is to stop run- away horses by jumping up and seizing them by the bridle. It is said that this animal has already saved the lives of eight persons, if not more.

_ Pautland, a Great Dane, received a collar for saving his mistress from the attack of a footpad, and Turk, a splendid Newfoundland, has had a similar honour for rescuing young children from drowning on several occasions.
THIS WEEK'S STORY. A THIRD-CLASS FACE.

A railway director recently entered a first-class carriage of the railway he controlled. Soon after he was seated he was accosted by a ticket collector. "Ticket, please," said the worthy. "1 haven't one," replied the director. "Then you must come out of that." "Oh, no. My face is my ticket, my good man." "Is it ?" snapped the
collector. "Then all I can say is that you are travelling first-class with a third-class ticket."
The then director wished he hadn't been BO funny.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 8 1911.
It is not very probable THE that Mr. LLOYD- POLITICAL GEORGE under-rated SITUATION, the difficulty of his task

when be introduced his National Insurance Bill to the House of Commons. On the contrary, he seems to have considered beforehand every possible objection. As we have already noted, he appears to be prepared for every variety of criticism, and for the examination, even to the minutest details, of his measure. What he may not have calculated upon is the use- less expenditure of time that must take place where each of several members of the House insists on standing sponsor to the same objection. Again, the CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER suggested on Wednesday, that members anxious about details should come to an understanding among themselves as to the nature of the infore,ation they desire to extract from him. A possible resort to the use of the guillotine has been deferred; but it is urgently necessary that some time- saving devices should be employed if the Bill is to he passed into law during the present session of Parliament, and it is obvious that what the CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER suggested is ono of the best and most effective. As he reminded the House, he has been anxious to clear up every detail of his scheme. He has invited rather than discouraged criticism ; and has on more than one occasion gone out of his way to meet his critics face to face. The result has been the removal of great masses of not very well-considered objections to his measure. But there must still be much give and take before the way is cleared for the third reading; and those members who may have objections to urge, but who are mainly anxious that the Bill should pass into law, will be well advised if they agree together as to which of their points are essential, so that as little as possible of the time of the House may be thrown away over matters that are not of real consequence. What took p!ace in the House of Lords on Wednesday night was interesting rather than important. As was pointed out some days since, Lord LANSIXAVNE's proposed clause lost all its significance when Lord CROMER'S amendments were carried. But we do not on that account begrudge the time that has been expended in discussion over subsequent amendments. The House of Lords has been explaining itself to the country; and we trust that it has been receiving the attention it deserves. Its position has, we think, been made admirably clear. There may be differences between Lord•LattsnowNE and some of those who sit behini him; but they are soundly agreed as to the assertion of the right of the House of Commons to be the first power in the State:

Two or three years ago nobody could have dreamed of such pretensions as are now being put forward. Even the wildest conjecture would not have surmised that the Conserva- tive Leader in the tipper House would make himself responsible for a proposal that a com- mittee of fourteen should be set up as the supreme authority over both Houses. We are living in an area of almost daily surprises; but nothing is more strange than a House which has declared its own unfitness to legis- late so long as it is constructed on the here- ditary basis, setting itself to devise means for excluding the people from any direct influ- ence on legislation. The late Sir WILLIAM GILBERT could hardly have devised such a I situation. However, the whole spirit of it is IGilbertian. It does not belong to the world 'of realities to which we must necessarily I return in a few days' time

On 'page three of this STATE INSURANCII issue we publish tWo AND 'rife valuable informative INFIRMARIES. reports on the possible effects of State Insur- ance on the Warrington Infirmary and other similar institutions. The reports have been drawn up for the consideration of the Board of Management, by Mr. W. P. Rylands and Messrs. G. R. Crosfield and J. H. Smethurst. The reports are agreed in finding that the proposals of the State Insurance Bill will inevitably (if the Bill becomes law) result in diminished contributions to Infirmaries and Hospitals. It is obvious that employers who are compelled to provide medical attend- ance, medicine and sick allowance for their workpeople, will find it impossible to continue their voluntary sub- scriptions to Infirmaries and the like. The same reasoning applies with equal force to the workers themselves. Instead of con- tinuing to be generous helpers of the local Infirmary they will find that the national contribution for State Insurance absorbs all the coppers that can be spared for such contingencies. Naturally, therefore, the governors of our Infirmary, and gentlemen in similar positions all over the country,view with alarm and dismay the possible crippling of the institutions which have done so much for the suffering poor. A conference has been held, and a memorial presented to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, urging among other things of importance, that the Bill shall be extended so as to provide for the recoup- ing of hospitals for the treatment of persons voluntarily or compulsorily insured by the Bill. This would meet the difficulties to some extent, but Mr. Rylands has come to the conclusion that " the inevitable consequences of this Bill must be the transfer of all hospitals to State management, as is the case in Germany " keeping with the present-day tendency for the State to control and guide our footsteps from the cradle to the grave." There perhaps, a little bitterness and undue pessimisim underlying Mr. Rylands' conclu- sions. For many reasons we think it would be a very good thing if the voluntary Infirmaries and Hospitals did come under State control. They confess to a state of chronic poverty (not always extreme, of course) and Warrington people at any rate, have realised very fully in recent years what a serious burden upon the locality our Infirmary is. The Million Penny Fund, and other appeals, have almost dried up the founts of charity, and many other deseriving objects are languishing for support which might readily be their's were the claims of the Infirmary not so insistent and so vast. It may well be that State Insurance heralds the dawn of a new day for the Infirmaries and Hospitals, and who shall say that that day will not be full of bright- ness and promise? State, instead of voluntary, control could hardly be an unmixed evil, and we shall await with interest Mr. Lloyd George's solution of a problem that he may view from a totally different standpoint from that of the memorialists.

The debeate upon Mr. SOME FEATURES Butcher's amendment OF THE DECLARA- to the Naval Prize TION DEBATE Bill—a debate which ranged over every point of the Declaration of London—was not lacking in features of interest. Mr. McKinnon Wood greatly enhanced his reputation by his lucid and cogent exposition. Mr. Wyndam and Mr. Leslie Scott made the notable admis- sion from the Opposition side of the House that we shall benefit substantially by the Declaration as neutrals. Mr. Holt, speak- ' ing as the head of one of the largeBt shipping firms in the United Kingdom, bore testimony to the advantages which our shipping trade would derive from the Declaration. Lord Charles Beresford, in a frank avowal that he and his naval colleagues would in time of war be ready to stretch a point and seize ships carrying food to an enemy, even if it was doubtful that the food came under the head of conditional contraband, as defined by the Declaration, blew Out of the water the contention of the Opposition that there was no danger, if the Declaration was not ratified, of other Powers treating food destined for the civil population as contraband. Mr. McKenna retorted crushingly to the challenge of the Opposition to bring forward the opinion of the Admiralty experts. Sir Edward Grey called the attention of the House to a vital point in the Declaration which the Opposi- tion had totally ignored. In embodying the British view of blockade it gives us an enormous advantage as belligerents, without whi:ll our command of the sea would be almost reduced to impotence. Mr. Asquith let fly a most galling shaft which penetrated a most vulnerable spot in the armottr of the Opposition when he alluded to the new-born 'zeal of the Tories for the importation of food I from foreign sources, and asked what had become of Tariff Reform.
4 Sir Edward Grey, in a THE FOREIGN speech of tremendous
SECRETARY ON force, cleared away the THE DECLARATION. huge.massof.nth3repr.e-

seniation which the Opposition speakers, and not least amongst them Mr. Balfour,have indulged in, whilst he opened up many new points of view. lie showed that without the Declaration we should be unable to induce neutrals to submit to the measures which would be necessary if we were to maintain an effective blockade. The vexed question of conversion of merchantmen into warships on the high seas is not affected by the Declaration. We stand just as we did. neither better nor worse. Mr. Balfour has taken up the attitude that in diplomatic pressure we had a better instrument for securing our interests as neutrals than in the tribunal and mks established by the Declaration. But Sir Edward Grey pointed out that it was the failure of the British Government—a Tory Government—to pre- vent the sinking of British vessels and to obtain adequate redress for it during the Russo-Japanese war that had driven home the necessity of such an instrument as the Declaration provides.

Mr. Asquith summed MR. ASQL-11-11'S up the case in a speech SUMMARY, that was a masterpiece of compression. (1) The Declaration, enlarging as it does the area of settled rules of international law, is an important new factor making (or the peace of the world. (2) The new code impairs our rights neither as belligerents nor neutrals. (3) The Declaration is supported by the expert naval advisers of the Admiralty, by two of the greatest Sea Lords of our time, and by all our great jurists with one exception whilst the Imperial Confer- ence, without a single dissentient voice, passed a resolution approving of it. (4) The Declaration gives us (a) the means of enforc- ing an effective blockade, (b) the free list of raw materials, (c) immunity from capture of food supplies for the civil population.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
"Chayos" is the latest addition to the vocabulary coined by one of our "City fathers."
"White fellow long rest" is the Australian motives' idea of Sunday observance, according to the Bishop of Perth who spoke at the Parr Hall, on Thursday.
Mr. C. E. Parker has boldly written an .article criticising compulsory military service. We suppose we shall now have to "prepare for cavalry." The N.S.L. never turns the other cheek!

Letter-cards impressed with Id. stamps of George V. design are now being placed on sale at post offices, price id. each. White material has bean substituted for the blue formerly used, and an alteration has been made in the perforation with the object of facilitating the opening of the cards. • •

Boy Scouts have !an-g since ceased to be a national joke. They have proved their capacity for serious application to duty and the most flattering comments were heard on the smart, soldierly appearance of the Warrington troop which returned proudly from the King's Review on Wednesday afternoon.

• • The Rev. Charles Brown, the president of the Free Church Council, announces in the " Ferme Park Magazine," that the M'Master University, Montreal. has conferred the degree of ' doctor " on him. He adds : I do not however, wish to be "doctored " by my own people. I would even drop the title of " Rev. ' if I could.

The King and Queen of Spain are expected to arrive at Cowes on a private visit to Eng- land on the 29th or 31st, and during the second weak in August they will be the guests of the Duke and Duchess of West- minster at Eaton Hall, Cheshire. King Alfonso is to proceed from Eaton to Scotland. and pay some visits for grouse-shooting and deer-stalking. •

- The strike scenes in Manchester and Salford demanded the augmentation of the local police forces with detachments from neighbouring towns. On Tuesday night Warrington sent forty men, in charge of Inspector Foster, and up to last evening they had not returned. We hear, however, that they have not been embroiled in any serious disturbances or sustained any personal injuries. • • The London correspondent of the Madrid newspaper' A.8.C." says : " Lord Asquith, the new Prime Minister, is working actively in the organisation of his Cabinet. This morning he had interviews with several important personalities, among whom were Mr. &mat, Under-Secretary of the Interior, Mr. Mackinon, M.P., lord Bauchan, and mister Kunaman, Secretary of the Treasury." • •

Probably few people could say off-hand when Liverpool and Birmingham were first connected by railway. The date was July 4th, 1837, and the line was called the Grand Junction Railway. Not one person in a thousand realises that this line was used for traffic within a fortnight of Queen Victoria's accession. The railway mania, which was the beginning of so many of the trunk lines now existing, did not rage, of course, until the middle of the forties,

Mr. and Mrs. A. H. brosfield gave a dinner party• at 39, Hyde Park gate, London, on Saturday night, and entertained the follow- ing guests :—The Grand Duke Boris, the Grand Duke Michael, Countess Torby, Countess Zia de Torby, the Greek Minister and Mrs. Gennadius, Baron George de Meyendorff, Baroness de Meyendorff, Lady Beatrice Kemp, Mrs. Barclay, M. Vouros, Colonel and Mrs. Beddington, Miss Sch ilizzi, and Dr. St. Clair Thompson. * * *

Warrington ladies.- will feel inclined to memorialize the Local Government Board when they read that the Inspector, at the end of the inquiry into the proposed Baths extensions, remarked that " baths are a bit of a luxury," and he would have to mention the matter to the Board. The proposals include a new ladies' swimming bath 58 feet long,and a second class men's bath 77 feet long. At present the ladies have to disport themselves in a shallow tank, that even a walrus would snort at with disgust. There is no improve- ment more urgent in Warrington than the extension of bathing facilities.

" It's a hareoplane" !—" Not it, it's a crow"! These were some of the remarks heard in Bewsey-street about half-past three yesterday afternoon, where a crowd of people were observed to be gazing skyward with great intentness. But it was an aeroplane after all. The rapidly-receding, bird-like object going westward at a great altitude was the monoplane of Mr. Melly, a Liverpool aviator, who, yesterday morning, flew from Waterloo to Manchester in 40 minutes, and was on his return journey when observed by the curious and sceptical Warringtonians.

The Mayor favoured the Council on Tues- day with a very interesting account of his visit to Westminster Abbey for the Corona- tion, and some of the newspapers favoured him with a little journalistic imagination which was not to the liking of so precise a a gentleman as Councillor Dr. Joseph. Referring to the difficulties of getting from the Abbey to other parts of the City his Arorship said that he was exceptionally fortunate and though he travelled ten miles to reach his hotel, which was only three- quarters of a mile away, he was half-an-hour on his railway journey back before some of the peers and peeresses reached their homes in the West End. Our contemporary stated That the Mayor was half-way home by this time, while a daily paper said that he had actually reached Warrington. Thus does .imagination out-run even the fastest express!

Almost every great city is turning its attention to town-planning in the spread of its suburbs. In America, as in our own country, the idea of garden cities and suburbs, and above all the necessity of looking forward in the matter, has caught hold of the public imagination, and an important Town-Planning Congress was held at Philadelphia the other day, which extended a cordial invitation to Mr. John Burns to explain his town- planning schemes on the other side of the Atlantic. And now Paris has taken up the idea of making some provision for the spread of her outskirts, and the last act of the recent Mayor of Paris, M. de Selves, before quitting office was to create a Commission for study- ing the problem. M. de Selves declared it necessary to create some methodical and harmonious plan for the extension of Paris, a plan that would take account of all the Awe& of the capital, social,economic, hygienic, and artistic, and not leave the development .of Paris to chance.

The Liberal campaign in Warrington pro- ceeds apace and the open-air meetings held during the past week have been largely attended and full of enthusiasm. Here as in every part of the country, one finds the workers eager for the passing into law of the Parliament Bill, which, by destroying the Lords' absolute veto, will open the way to more much-needed social legislation and the remedying of abuses and anomalies. • • _ _ _ . • . _ . . .

Most of the local Church of England Parish Magazines for ,the current month comment severely or sarcastically on the lack of a civic service in church on the morning of Corona- tion Day. There is a big divergence of opinion on what was necessary and practic- able between, say, the Parish Church and the Town Hall, and relationships are under- stood to be somewhat strained. The man in the (Warrington) street has heard just about enough of the Coronation—and still claims to be loyal !

One of the most notable features of the diocesan missionary festival at Warrington on Thursday was the vigorous defence of toreign missions by Colonel Kelly, a respected officer who has seen much service in other lands. The part of his address which aroused most sympathy was his reference to the isolation of the missionary, often a highly educated University man, who, from sheer devotion to his work, is content to pass his days amid utterly uncongenial surroundings, far away from all civilized society. Such self-sacrifice naturally won the admira- tion of Colonel Kelly, who has often been an eye-witness of the missionary's heroic devotion, and now that he is in the old country he is not satisfied with a tacit support of missions but is ready to plead their cause with sincerity and power on public platforms. _ _

We quote the following paragraph from Mr. W. H. R. Curtler's " Short History of English Agriculture," as a warning to those who imagine that Tariff Reform would be the salvation of British Agriculture : In 1815 Protection reached its bigbevt limit, the Act of that year prthibiting import of wheat when the price was under SO shillings a querter, sad other grain in proportion. However, it was of no avail, and in the beginning of MI6 the complaints of agricultural dietres• were ett load and deep that the Board of Agri- culture issued circular letters to every part of the kingdom asking for information on the state of agriculture. According to the answera given rent had already fallen twenty•fire rer cent. ; ard agriculture Was in a ' deplorable state.' Bankruptcies, seizures,executions, imprisonments, were rife, many farmers had become parish paupers. Rent was much in arrtar, tithe and poor rates unpaid, improvements generally dis- continued, live mock chneiniehed ; alarming girls of poachers and other depredators rat rd the country." • Surely the reductio ad absurdum of tariffs is found in a German treaty with Switzer- land which contains a clause which deserves to remain famous. The treaty signed with Switzerland on the 12th November, 1904, admits into Germany at a reduced tariff the "bovine beast of the region of the high plateau of the mountains, belonging to the great spotted • race or to the brown race, which has been reared at an altitude of at least 300 metres above the level of the sea, and has made each year a sojourn of one month, at the minimum, at an altitude of at least 800 metres above the level of the sea." So careful had the German negotiators to be in order to exclude the French "bovine beasts." It seems hard on the cow that has been reared in the pleasant valleys of Switzerland that it must pay the higher duty. The picture of Mr. Balfour pursuing his policy of Retaliation and superintending negotiations of this sort is one which no doubt every Tariff Reformer would delight in.

div.head: LORD AND LADY ACTON GIVE GARDEN PAM.
div.p: LORD AND LADY ACTON GIVE GARDEN PAM.
HISTORIC GATHERING AT ALDENHAM PARK.
Speech by Mr. A H Crestleld.

Lirni and Lady Acton entertained the Liberals of Shropshire at • garden party at their beautiful old- world home. Aldenham Park, near Bridgncuth on Monday. Lord Acton, who is a lord-in•weiting to the King, was kept in London until Saturday evening, when, with Lady Acton (who is well remembered here as the daughter of Mr. T. H. Lyon), be came down to his Shropshire home for the garden party, which wan. largely brought about by the eff inn of Major Hamby, and held under the auspices of the Shropehire branch of the Liberal Social Council of which Lady Acton le President. Over a thousand invitations were accepted, and the guests arrived by moo:moors, carriage., and brakes from all the Parliamentary Dieiyio.s of the county. The day was delightfully fine and the beautiful surroundings of tie ha'l and the belt of woodland that sweeps away across the seven thousand acres !hot make up the estate were seen at their best. The in tin b dy of the preeeut h nIl wan built in 1691. But the family had their Neat at Ahleaharn before that. The trot baronet of the line was Edward .teton of Altienham, who for his loyalty to Charles 1 wan made a baronet in 1043. His wife was Sarah, daughter of Richard Mytton of Halidon. Several of the succeeding baronets reprei.ented ftridgnorth in Parlianaent. The family is descended from William Act 11. deActon Rumen, who lived in the reign of Edward 111. The nret baron was the great Lord Acton, whom wonder- ful library was bequeathed to Lard Morley; while the present baron has corned in the diplomatic c ,rps in most of the principal capitals of Europe, and left Alilenhain the following day to resume duty at the Hague. On arriving the guests were received by Lady Acton and Lady Roxburgh, nod efterwards palmed into the house and out on to the beautiful lawna and into the old Englieh flower gardens. Later, tea woe served in the library and other rooms. At nix p.m. the vieitors massed round the front of the hall to listen to a little speech-making. 'I lie prim, pals took nip their places on the steps leading to the entrance, from which a fine view is obtained of the hall-mile sweep of drive running between an avenue of lofty elms, with the park of 170 acres stretching away all round.

„._. Lady Amon, who was received with applause. said it gave Lord Acton and her great pleasurelo welcome them to Aldenham on behalf of the Liberal Social Council. represented the,. by Lady Roxburgh, who had m-st kindly come down from Landon for the purpose. (Applatme.) She was sure it would gratify the Liberal Social Council very much to learn how many Liberals there were is thst part of Shropshire (applause)—• part they so often beard sirAen of in viessentiall • Tory stroogh Id. (Laughter and a Voice 'Plural voters.”) She would like to say how delighted Lord Acton and she were por.ronslly to have the opportunity of rreeiving so many of their fellow countrymen and country woolen. After a speech by Ludy Roxburgh, Mr. A. H. Crasfield .I°l,olol a capit .1 ad frees, in 'the coarse of which he Raid he felt it was something like • proud privilege to be a member of the Liberal party in such great and encouraging days as those in which they now lived. (Applauae). Referring to the Veto Bill, Mr. Crosfield sod they did mit mean to abolish Second Chamber goveloment, but to give both parties in the State more equality of opportunity—(A Voice " Fair play ")—in s word, more fair play. The Liberal party intended to do that. (Applause). The Second Chamber would still retain great power and influence, but this inequality, thin unchecked vi to they would do away with absolutely. (Loud applause).

After other speeches and vote. of thanks to the host and hostess and Mr. Crosfield for his satire. Laid Acton, on coming to the front to respond, was received with prolonged cheerir g. Ile add it was a source of much gratification to Lads Acton and himself that the first gnat meeting of Liberals in the county should be held at his aocient home, the house where the idea of a History of Liberty waa first conceived. (Applause). It was most fitting and appropriate that they !Mould meet there at that moment, when an they hoped aml believed they were on the eve of victory, and were about to reap their harvest after labours extend- ing over many years. But if they were on the eve of victory he ventured ti hops—and he was saying this it his capacity of diplomatist and as keeper in a minor degree of the world s peace—he hoped that like all honourable victors they would remember to be generous to the other side in the hour of triumph, and above all bear in mind the fundamental axiom ef true Liberalism, the protection of minorities f ma ma jori.- tion. div.head: TRADE RETURNS.
div.p: TRADE RETURNS.
BIG RISE IN EXPORTS AND FALL IN IMPORTS.
The Board of Trade returns for last month show that the imports amounted to £50,105,889, as compared with £54,629,818 for the corresponding month of last year, or a Idecrease of £3,523,928.

The total exports during last month reached a value of £36,113,150 as against £34,799,654 for the month of June last, an increase of £1,313,496. For the six months ended June 30, the imports totalled £334,124,058, a decrease of £282,393 as compared with the corresponding period of the previous year. The exports for the six months ended last month, amounted to £223,668,297, an increase over the corresponding six months last year of £19,082,574.
COTTON EXPORTS UP. The exports of manufactured cotton for last month show an increase of nearly .£650,000, as compared with the corresponding lmonth last year.

Special reference was made at the Wycliffe Congre- -1 national Church on Sunday evening by the 1t... John Yonge touching the late Mr. Francis Brown, who was a prominent member of that congregation. Taking his tent from " A good name in rather to be chosen than great flame ; end loving favour rather than silver and gold" (Prov. mi. I) end 'A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of one's birth" (Boehm. vii. Ilia reason for selecting those verses for that memorial sermon men the fact that tiwir lately deported friend bad, in the opinion of •Il who knew him, tucceesfull) won for him- self the distinguished hmoor of "A 0000 Nom".

Time who knew him would &ways cherish se memory as that of a man who erdeerned character se the most desirable of achievements, and be had always, so for a. any of them knew, striven to do Lie duty in the sphere of life to which Providence had celled him animated by the true fear of God and desiring the welfare of those among whom his lot wan cast. In the sisy.of his health and vigour, no one, in their Wycliffe community, bad leer • more devoted, diligent, constant member, anther, servant or brother, than he (Mr. Brown). The habit of his life warr to hold the church of his Saviour and Muter supreme in hi. atroogest regard. So long.. ever it nes pornible, he sat, Sunday by Sunday, twice In the day, labia seat, with his strong, manly steadfut eyes, ever fixed upon that pulpit, et hi, inner eye. were ever constantly viewing the presence of the Lord. Week- day and Sunday his feet bore him there. Whoever else was absent, he was present. Whoever else was irregular and wayward in attendance he was diligently consuot. div.head: LAND OF DEAL PRISONS.
div.p: LAND OF DEAL PRISONS.
IN JAPAN WOMEN CRIMINALS ARE TAUGHT DAINTINESS AND DEPORTMENT.

It is difficult to associate the light-hearted, child- like Japanese women with the dark, for- bidding and depressing side of life suggested by 1 prison. But even in the Land of the Rising Sun crime and the punishment of it have to be reckoned with ; and the question of reform- ing women criminals is a prominent one in Japan just now. An American who visited one of the chief prisons for women in Japan was much struck with the curative system in vogue. "There I are," he says, "no massive buildings and glass windows with iron bars, no bare stone floors, no long corridors and tiny cells where the prisoners spend long hours of solitary confinement. The buildings surround a central courtyard, and are built of wocden planks or standards, cage fashion, so that the prisoners are living an open air life day and night. The floors are covered with corn calored matting, and the woodwork is polished till every grain is visible. The prisoners wear pink crepe kimonos, which contrast with their ivory faces and gleaming hair.

"We were taken to one large room where three rows of pink clad figures were squatting Japanese fashion on pink cushions on the floor. They greeted us with shy smiles and soft murmurs of ' Ohayo,' the Japanese ' Good day,' while they simul- taneously bowed their blue black heads to the ground. Politeness is one of the chief virtues in Japan, and in the prisons special lessons are given in manners and deportment, and classes are even held to teach the art of tea serving, which is an important ceremony with the Japanese. The idea is that what- ever raises the self-respect of the prisoner, whatever improves her behaviour and manners, aids her reformation. The teach- ing is very comprehensive. Lessons are given in weaving, dressmaking and sewing, and we saw some exquisite embroideries made in the prison and artistic garments cut kimono fashion.

"The prisoners work in sheds all day, aid that the cells are practically sleeping apart- ments, and it has been found that working in association under official control makes for reform and improvement of mental and physical health. Prison in Japan is an educa- tional agency and the women work and are paid wages for what they do. Prizes and decorative awards are also given as an incentive to good work and conduct.

_ "The Japanese of to-day could teach us a great deal in the matter of penology. They allow their prisoners more liberty, they show a more sympathetic interest in their welfare, than we do. Everything is done to teach them industry and morality. As their behaviour improves they are given better food and various privileges. Everything and every prisoner is scrupulously clean."

div.head: PILGRIMAGES MALPAS AND THE BIRTHPLACE OF BISHOP HEBER.
div.p: PILGRIMAGES MALPAS AND THE BIRTHPLACE OF BISHOP HEBER.
Our own plan for reaching Ma!pas was leisurely and luxurious, and on that account, of course, to be commended.

The More strenuous cyclist may ponder over his map and choose a way for himself; ours lay through the domain of the Duke of Westminster, and included a leisurely dawdle and tea-drinking interval, the description of which would only incite envy.

Dropping from the train at Balderton Bridge, we picked our way through the glades of the outer Eaton Park, faced the two mile avenue that leads to the gates of the Hall, and then turned aside to bask by ,1 the river side amid the beauties of the spot 1 known (it merits a prettier name) as the Iron Bridge. It deserves to be widely known that while the Duke will have none of those snorting monstrosities known as motor bikes, the innocent cycle may travel any- where within the Park.

The road to Holt seemed shockingly dusty (the Park had made us fastidious), and it wa3 a relief to dismount and go a hunting acrcza green fields, the object of the hunt being the Roman station that stands on the banks of the Dee not far from the fine old- world bridge that joins up Holt and Farndon. But we shall crowd up our article unduly if we get back to the Roman age. We must only consent to linger at the next stopping place, the old Cheshire village of Malpas. UALPAS.

Possibly Malpaa would call itself a town. We will not quarrel ; it is enough that it has one glimmer of fame and that as long as people sing' From Greenland's icy mauntains" it will be a place of pilgrimage. It was at the Higher Rectory, so called to distinguish it from the present Rectory, that Reginald Heber was blrn. The village can tell us little concerning him save to point to the room where he first saw the light and tell us that the font from which he was baptized has been carried from Malpas and is now the font of St. Chad's, Shrewsbury. But we feel no dissatisfaction that there is little to see. In this old place Heber received his first impressions and began a life that was to carry untold inspiration and leave lasting sweetness behind.

Reginald Heber was born here on April 21st, 1783. His father had married twice and of the first marriage was Richard, one of the most remarkable bibliophiles of his day, a man indeed who seemed to feel no interest at all in life save that of book gathering and whose doings make a curious story. Reginald was the eldest son of the second marriage and showed early signs of quick intellect. When he went to Brazenose College, Oxford, in 1800, after some early years spent at the Whitchurch Grammar School he took the College by storm. In poetry especially he found excellence, and when the Duke of Wellington was installed as Chancellor one of Heber's poems " Palestine," was recited to the immense and distinguished audience. This was a great triumph for a youth of eighteen and the poem was warmly praised by Sir Walter Scott, who was on a visit to the University City.

Whilst the poem was in course of composition it happened that Sir Walter Scott came to breakfast with Heber and his brother. " Palestine" became the subject of conversation and Heber read it aloud. "You have omitted "said Sir Walter—" one strik- ing circumstance to your account of the building of the temple, that no tools were used in its erection." Reginald retired from the table to a corner of the room and added the lines which by many are regarded as the most beautiful of all :
No hammer fell, no pooderone axes rung Like some's!i pilm the myetic fabric sprang Efajeatic silence ! _ _

After five years at Oxford he took his Arts degree and then following the fashion of the period took a Continental tour. On his return he was ordained and put into the family living as Vicar of Hodnet in Salop. The same year he marriect Miss Amelia Shipley, daughter of the Dean of St. Asaph and thus at the age of twenty-four entered upon a life for which he was admirably equipped both by learning and sympathy.

div.head: HEBER AS HYMN WRITER:
div.p: HEBER AS HYMN WRITER:

It was during the early years of his ministry that he turned his thoughts to the writing of hymns. From the year 1811 to the end of his life he cherished the idea of a recognised Church Hymn Book—a scheme which came to fruition in " Hymns Ancient and Modern "—and towards this he made some fine contributions. Among those which are likely to last are the hymns : Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty. Jesus Christ is rises to-day. Brightest sod best are the sons of the morning. Lord of Mercy sod of Night. The Soo of Ood g es forth to war.
But none of these have attained the extraordinary popularity of his missionary verses
From Orsonland's icy mountains.

The hymn dates from Whitsuntide 1819. Heber was on a visit to his wife's father, Dean Shipley, at Wrexham, and on Whit Sunday there was to be held a special service of the Society tor the Propagation of the Gospel. The idea of writing a Missionary hymn was suggested by the Dean and on the Saturday afternoon Heber wrote the three first stanzas adding a little later in ths day the fourth stanza. We sing the hymn just as it came from his pen save that he originally wrote

- - What thoug the .pie 7 bream Blow soft o'er Jara's ! The curious traveller may see the room in which the hymn had its birth, for the old Rectory was swallowed in the scheme for making a railway through the town and the company with commendable economy adopted the house as a booking office and the windows, in the recess of which Heber sat to pen the verses, remain unchanged.

div.head: HEBICE AS BISHOP.
div.p: HEBICE AS BISHOP.

I Honours ca-m-e--to-lie-be'r-Fro-m. the Church of which he was a devoted son, the greatest being that of the offer of the Bishopric of Calcutta. He was too thoughtful a man to receive the honour lightly and it came to him as the greatest test and crisis of his life. It should be remembered, of course, that the post was practically that of a superintendent missionary. India had only just been opened by the labours of Carey and Marshman and only one Anglican Bishop had been sent out -the one whose pla.e he was asked to fill. It meant in reality being the only Bishop in the Eastern Hemisphere for the sea of Calcutta had no boundariee, Hebei' was then 19 years old and felt that he dare not accept the great responsibility, a feeling that was increased by the knowledge of the danger to health that might come to his wife and child. Rut missionary real conquered 4nd he sailed in June Ifi2d,reaching India after four months of travel his" Indian Journal "describe; much that he saw and endured during the brief years

he was allowed to labour. It begins on the day he left England to terminate abruptly in March 1826. Three weeks from this date he was at rest for ever from the toils of his great parish. Two and a half years only he spent in India but he filled them with labours that make one of the greatest chapters in the history oft he English Church. He had completed a long and laborious visitation in 1825 and in the early months of 1826 started again on the same errand. In April he had reached Trichinopoly and had spent Sunday and Monday in preaching and visitation. On the Monday evening he took a warm bath after an exhausting day and was found by his servant dead in the water overtaken by a stroke of apoplexy.

div.head: BISHOP HEBER:g LEGACY OF LOVE.
div.p: BISHOP HEBER:g LEGACY OF LOVE.

Bishop Heber continued to live in India as in England by the fine spirit and real sym- pathy that he had revealed through life. His Journal shows how broad his charities were towards the men he met abroad and with what fine skill he managed to see things as others saw them.

It is proverbial that the Mission field is the best place to get rid of church exclusiveness and if Heber had carried from England any Anglican narrowness he would quickly have lost it in the presence of the work he took up in Calcutta, for he followed in the footsteps of William Carey and was in a very real sense one of his successors. It is good to read the letter he wrote in June 1824 after witnessing the work of Carey and Hershman in which he affectionately describes the two Baptiste as his " honoured brethren" and his superiors both in age and talent." Like many other high churchmen he learned abroad what few of his class seem to learn at home that exclusiveness is a great barrier to the Gospel. He wrote after his experience in India, "If a re-union of our churches could be effected, the harvest of the heathen would ere long be reaped, and the work of the Lord would advance among them with a celerity of which we have now no experience."

Sual frankness and sincerity always win the heart, and Heber died lamented and beloved in the land °lbis adoption. A native admirer did not exaggerate in saying that "His virtues rendered his course of life a track of light the admiration of Britain and India."

These memories come with the greater strength as we survey the spot where his unstained life began and we travel in imagination to Trichinopoly where a stone marks the place of his burial: Sacred t , the memory of Regina,rl Reber PD , 11 Lord Bishop of Caleu to who so m here called to I his eternal te.t during his vhitation of the Sosthero Pmvineea of his extensive di car, on the 3rd ef April 1A26. We remember too the inscription placed to his memory in St. Paul's Cathedtal. .

To the mernwy of Reginald Heber D D., thin monument was erected by those who loved and admired him. His charowter exhibited a rare mesaure of fervent zeal with universal tolerance, of brilliant talent with sober judgment, and wan eepecially distiogniehed by Christian humility which no applause could disturb,no omens abate. He cheerfully resigned prnspects of eminence at home is order to become the chief minsionary of Christianity in the East, and having is the short !pace of three yearn 'hilted the greater part of India and con, dinned the affection and veneration of men of every class of religion, he was there summoned to receive the rewnri of his labours in the 41rt1 year of his age, 1826. _

He marched. up to the far end Of the long room, called • waitress who had often served him before, and naked her to get him • small table which he could have alone. .

- ...... . She did o after a very little difficulty. Ile sank into his seat, ordered • simple dinnot with a pint of stout, and sat back waiting lot it. One or two people who knew him elightly, nodded to him. Ile nodded in reply, his insolence growing more marked each time he saw a chance acquaintance.

Presently he took up a paper and pre- tended to bury himself in its contents. While he did No, however, he kept one hand in his pocket, and that hand elatTed the letter marked "Teheran," and addressed to old Mr. Itenshall.

....... The girl brought him his dinner. Ile ate in an abstracted manner, paid his bill, and went out. Ile now took an omnibus, mounted on the roof, and was borne in the direction of Islington. lie was put down after half an hour's rids in a somewhat obscure part of that vast suburb. Ile walked down a side street. crossed a square, entered another street, and stopped before a aliabby Wows. lie took a latch key from his pocket and let himself in. If the house was shabby in its exterior, it was still more no inside. The hall was long and narrow, ill furnished, with torn linoleum on the floor, and a very dull gas jet throwing but a feeble glimmer of light up the dark staircase. Deeps., however, was accustomed to these squalid surroundings. Ile ran up- stairs, three steps at a time, and presently found himself in a sort of bed-Aitting room f:rf the poorest description at the top of the house.

There was a feeble fire burning in the grate. Ile turned on some incandescent light, which made his room at once cotnparatively cheerful, pulled down the blinds with a jerk, and, taking a small saucepan from a cup- board in the wall, filled it with water. Ho put the saucepan on the fire in order that the water might get hot. When it smoked and steamed he held the foreign letter marked "Teheran" over it, raised the flap gingerly. and took the contents from the envelope. He had locked his door, and was sure of being uninterrupted. The letter was in the same manly writing which eharacteriAed the address on the enve- lope. The paper was thin and foreign.

- - "Dear Mr. }tensilell," it ran. "I shall be in England, and will call upon you the end of February. I expect to get to England about the 20th of the month and will go straight to your business address—the ad- dress you gave me in Teheran seven years ago. I am bringing you back the five hun- dred pounds you were so generous as to lend me, and the full interest on the money. In return, I am anxious to secure the diamond. When we have made our exchange we shall be quita—that is. in one sense; but I shall never, as long as I live, forget your kimlneps and how you helped a man through a tight corner and set him on his legs. You must have thought that I was lost during all these years of silence, but when we meet, I shall have a strange tale to tell you—one which I dare not whisper on this paper. I can, how- ever, say that I have been in prison and in peril of my life, and that even now I am a hunted man. I shall not be safe or able to breathe freely or to enjoy the fact that I am only twenty-niqe years of age until I hold that diamond in my clasp ind give it to the one who demands it back. "Independently of all these things, how- ever, you may be glad to hear that the money which saved me and which you so nobly lent in- has borne excellent fruit, and I come to England with • considerable tor- ten.. All I need now, therefore, is to make things straight with von and to put things straight for myself.—tours, with everlasting gratitude. GEHAHD LONSDALE."

Deepe read this letter over once—twice. Then he got up and, going to bin mantel- ieee looked at the clock. It was still com- paratively early; not quite ten. He felt ex- cited. The contents of the letter stimulated him, lip said to himself that he always sus- pected a mystery. He had served for a war of his life as a clerk in the office of Itobert Ilensh•11, and, although he was forced to resign thin em- ployment owing to circumstance. which Beli- sha)! never spoke of, he had made good use of his opportunities. He was the sort of man whose observation is so keen that nothing recap. hint, npd whose memory in no good that be remembers the most minute detail.. _
"Ah," he said to hirnself, on thi; "I begin to get a Flimmer of Itenshall's strange interest in leheran, in Persia, in the Shah.'

Again he looked at the clock. "The diamond!" le murmured. "That fel- low cornea back with a fortune, lie wants the diartlond, he is afraid; why? Ile says he is hunted. He confeases to having spent some at his time ia prima. The diamond will put him right. Suppose he never get. it. Suppose I eee Mary to-night—yes, to- night." Deepe matched up his hat, thrust it on his 'head, turned off the gas and ran dr...Weirs. Ile wax a poor man who counted his money by shillings, but so excited was he now that ho gave himself the luxury of a hansom all the wny from Islington to Paddock Row. Robert Henshall crept slowly home after • long day's work in the city. He was a man of about fifty yearn of age, but had a sloop, and white hair, sod a somewhat haggard face. He reached ilin't,Wll house goon alter six o'clock, let himeelf in with a latch key, and called in a querulous tone: "Mary Gray! Where are you?" His voice penetrated through the small house. There earn.: an answering tone, quite bright and cheerful, and a girl of about five- nod-twenty, dressed very neatly, and with hair bound simply round her shapely head, opened the door and came into view. am not well," was the reply. "I want • fire to be lit at once in my room and some. thing hot prepared for me to drink. lit dinner—no dinner; I couldn't touch it. Old Robert Hermitsll straightened himself and looked full at the girl from under his shaggy pent-house brows. "Why on earth should you frfghten 13eeky? She is going out, as usual, I suppose?" "Yes; she is dressing now. Ike Lorrimers are taking her to a donee at the Town Hall, and she will dine with them first."

"Why aren't you going, Mary?" "I Prefer to stay at 'home and look aftet your comfort.. Mr. Belishall." "Alt, good girl!" said the old man. "Well, see about the fire and the hot drink. Let me know when my room is ready. I shall go intc my study until you tell me that everything is prepared." Mary nodded, and went in the direction of the kitchens. Her face, at a first glance, might have been thought pleasant. A second glance would have made the observer of that name face not quite no certain with regard to it, but a third glance would have reassured him. For Mary had the knack of never wear- ing her heart on her sleeve; in short, under too possible circumstances would she dream of giving herself away. She went to the kitchen now to give direc- tions, and the old man, well satisfied, dropped into a chair by the fire in his study. The house was small, but was kept in apple. 1. Is order. The fire bad just been made rip and burned brightly; the hearth was clean. Be tented on the electric light and spread out his limbs to the grateful warmth. "Ah!" he murmured; .it is a cold night even for the time of year; and %gm an old, old man, not in years, perhaps, at in—in, mind. I have bad a hard fight for it. I havei conquered, though, all the same. There is, plenty for Becky when I am gone. I am glad Becky in going to enjoy herself. I like to think that she ham never wanted for anything all the days of her life. Poor little Beck l—leff motherless at two years old and brought up by the old dad, and never, never, through all his wanderings and the many conflicting difficul. ties of his life wanting for anything. Poor, pretty, dear little Beek!" _

"And why should not I take an hoar's holi- day if I choose, miss," was the reply; mar. inured, however, in a tone of the deepest affection. "What is to hinder me if I can get through my work? I am a rich man, my little Rebecca, and could live in a big house if I pleased, and keeVdosens of servants. div.p: FREE TRADE LECTURE CAMPAIGN.

The Tariff Controversy ha. not been altogether fruit- less, inasmuch u it ha. stimulated general interest in economic aci,nce. The surest safeguard against Tariff Reform is the spread of economic knowledge. The Free Trade Union, recognising this,are taking advent ag of the opportunity afforded by the respite from acute propaganda, to carry out, during the corning autumn, • scheme of primly educational work In economics on university extension lines. Tbe Manchester Secretary, Mr. Samuel Gleave, Is just now completing hi, final plans for carrying oat the scheme in abed fifty centres in the North.Weatern Courtlier; The centres so fir selected include Moss Side, P, ndleton, Newton Heath, Les...huhu and Preto...lob in the Manchester district, Middleton, Altrincham, Sale, Heywood, Bury, Ilyde, Leigh, Stockport, Oldham, A.Moo,Stalybridge, Dances, Blackburn, Chorley, Preston, Bolton, Rochdale, Little- borough, fodniorden, Huddersfield, Bradford, Kendal, Londoner, Carlisle, Acorington Itawlenstall, Burnley, Warrington,Northwich,klacciesield,Glossopend ton. The lecturers will be university graduates who have I specialised in iconomica,and who have practical experi- ence in speaking and teaching. In preparing the plans Mr. Weave is profiting by the experienoe of the work- ing of experimental scheme. in past ...sons; and for the coming autumn will provide fur • wider selection of lecture. than in past Deane.. To scold overlapping and all unnecessary expenditure of sor ney (for the Union is hampered by extremely limited financial 'dour. s) the scheme will be worked SO far O. pusible in co-operation with local organiza- tion,. No duces sill be arranged without local guarantees of .saver's) attendance of fifty eluded, Ihe CiAMOS will not be confined to men ; w the contrary, the active help of ladies an secretaries, unvassem, end members of local committeea will be especially welcomed. Tbe students will be provided by the Free Trade Unied nub syllabuses, text books and weekly notes on the alibied. discussed, ends I irmiltaneous and properly conducted examination will be held at each cettre in the early pert of December. On the 'vault of the examirdion there will be &nerds of certificates and medals or prize. Demondrations will be orguiied at the most convenient dawn ; at which dlatieguished Frre Traders of national reputation will .peak, and distribute the awards to tunmessfull competitor.. Local organimtiorm deeiring to co-operate, as well as intend ing students and workers are in•ited to communicate with Mr. Samuel (Heave, at the oflioes of the Free Trade Union, North-Western Coutiee Branch, 82, Cross.st re et, Manchester.

div.head: Carbolic Acid in Tea.
div.p: Carbolic Acid in Tea.

A LYMNI CASE AT CHESTER ASSIZES. ACCUSED ACQUITTED. At the Chester Assizes on Wednesday, before ifr. Justice Eldon Banks nod. jury, Fred Jennings, aged 16, of Lm, fustian cutter, was charged with .• having maliciously administered to, or caused to be adruinia- tere.d to or taken by his sister Edna Jennings, carbolic . . . . . , . „

a...O.iFs;itl:lnTals-t-tbere-by to inj UM her." Mr. Harold Edwards (instructed by Mr. 11. L. Ilerris, ,of Alttiochmu) prow:rated and Mr. Austin L. Jones I (instructed by Mr. Thomas S. Steel, of Warrington) I defended. Counsel in opening the case against the prisoner stated that on the morning of Vie 17th of March lest the mother of the prisoner who bad been out all night nursing a sick psrson returned to the house where she found her husband sitting in the kitchen besting a drink of tea before he went to work. An elder son also had some tea with them and the father and son went to , their work. The tea that remained was left in the tea- pot neer the fire and the mother went to bed. The prisoner then got op and it seemed pretty clear, although there was no direct evidence of it exceyt the prisoner's admissions to the police afterwards, that the prisoner took a bottle containing carbolic acid used as a disinfectant fluid sod poured some into the teapot. He then oallt d his sister and left the house for his work. The girl got op, poured out for herself a cap of tea took a sip and .wallowed it. Smelling and tasting the carbolic acid in the tea she called bar mother who administered an emetic of salt and water. Information was given to the police, and after Inquiries, prisoner was interrogated, when be admitted that he had put aome carbolic acid in the lea. Edna Jennings bore out Counsel's statement but on cross-examination by Mr. Austin Jonas admitted that she could smell carbolic acid before she poured cot the tee from the pot into the cop and that she knew carbolic acid was poison. She had always been on friendly terms with her brother and she knew of no reason why he should attempt to poison her. She did not think he intended to do so. Maria Jennings, the prisoner's mother,stated that the carbolic had been used to put in whitewash and that it had been kept in the VI, of the cupboard. She could not account for prisoner's conduct. Crows-examined by Mr. Austin Jones witness said that prisoner left school when he was in the 4th standard. Ile was a dull boy hot she had alwa3e con- sidered him very harmless. Dr. Joseph Carter Bell (County Analyst for Cheshire) I stated that he had made an availsin of the contents of the bottle and teapot. The contents of the teapot consisted of weak tea meseurinf about one and a half pints. The liquid smelt of disinfecting fluid and con- taifted shout ten graine of crude carbolic acid to the pint and shall of tea. What was left in the teapot would not kill. Ile would not be afraid to take a cupful of the liquid. Cross-examined witness said that two or three drops only of the carbolic acid must have been put in the teapot. :So ill effects would be felt after drinking.

The Clerk re-a.cleiet-ter 1;;;,--ti;-E.Tcal Government Board encloeing a letter dated May 31st, received by them from Dr. S. .1. Parker, of Stockton Heath. The Board ached that they might be furnished with the Council*e observations on it. A scheme for the public health, the letter rao, such as you would like to see withie easy access of every town in England has been ineugurated by myself and others, do. —re open-air swimming beth. It is for any inspectors of the Local Government Board or any Medical Officer of lieslth to see it, and he will at orme extend to It his el:isolate approval an of the greatest moral end physical advantage to the community. . The "Stockton Heath Lake" as it is called is fed by a Ntream fortunately outside the ...fal- terers' zone, so that it cannot he coutaminsted by trade effluents. The Runcorn Rural Council are responsible for any contamination of it by sewage. Inasmuch as a property-owner of insanitary cottages in coetaminating this lake by nevrege by permitting the discharge of effluent from several foul cesspools into it, thereby violating tbe Public Health and other Sanitary Acts; and inasmuch as, having already notified the responsible unitary authority thereon, end have only received vague verbal information that some- thing may be done at the end of the summer, I appeal to the Local Government Board to know what my latitude should be in the matter. It seems to me the law is plain and concise. Uncleansed cesspool., the contents setureting the surrounding ground, are a nuissoce. Their effluent discharging into a stream or lake renders the offender liable to heavy penalties. The Sanitary Authority may be put in motion by any person aggrieved." The Clerk said that that matter came before the Council a little while ago and Mr. Pillieg Mr. Mclntyre and the Sanitary Inspector were requested to make an lest ection and report on the pollution of the stream which fed the lake. _ . . . . . .
