GREAT LABOUR DENIONSTRATION.

Between WOO and 12,00 workers from all parts of the Newton division took part ins demonstration et Haydock Park on Psturday. An interesting feature was the large turnout of members of the Women's Labour Lesgue as well as the Junior Labour League. The various sections met on the market square, Asbton-in-Makerfield, end accompanied by numerous bands, with many Hoe banners marched to the park, where meetings were held at two platforms. The resolution, which was carried with enthusiasm at both platforms, rejoiced at the prospect of the immediate passage into law of the Parliament Bill, and hoped that in this Parliament measures would also be pawed which would secure permanent peace between this country and the United States of America and other countries, the right to work, greater protection of life and limb in mines, the unrestricted right of trade unionsito engage in political activities whenever a majority of their members desired to do so, more ressooable hours of labour for shop assistants, the abolition of plural voting, and women's no if rage. It welcomed the Insurance Bill as a recognition of

eatlonel responeibility for sickness, invalidity and unemployment. bat asked for a.nendaente. Mr. J. lieir Hardie, M.P., said they would obeerve that during the peat week the House of Lords bed taken on. fresh lease of activity. He attributed that 'rarely to the fact that during the Coronation ceremony they had positiona of importance, positions of honour, positions of trust, whereas the representatives of the people in the House of Commons were treated as persons of no consequence. We heard a good deal shoot the possibility of another election thin year over the Veto. He did not believe in it ; there was no need for it. . . . . .

--lifir.-671;;;;;;;Vio,"ooTri—gratTil;tediCe ;;;;riters of the Newton division on having bad the common eeeee to allow the women to organise side by side with them To teference to the Parliamelt Bill he said that if the Government were in earnest there was no need for another election. What the House if Lords were Oct for was the defence of claw interest.. Lord Wollner was going to die in the last ditch againat the payment of members, but his family ought to In the last in the world to grumble against payments Oct of the puhlie ! purse. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. A. Seddon, who had a great reception, alluded to the Barham, nt Bill, and raid that if the Govern- ment slackened one inch from the provisions of the measure the worse it would be for then:rand the sooner would come shout the emancipation of the class which he represented. The provision, of the Veto Bill were the nvenimous demand of democracy. They had lived beyond the trappinge and mummeries of an effete aristocracy, and in the political life of this country wanted the ability, fertility, end stamina which the British claimed to have. (Hear, hear.) The ; Labour party were neither downhearted nor dismayed. He was glad the Lords were taking up their preeent attitude, and if they would only continue in their mad career, what the industrial democracy wanted would be realised sooner than they anticipated. (Applause). With reepect to the Insurarce Bill, It was not ell they wanted, bet they welcomed Its principle, and wanted the Government to recognise that the highest wealth of the nation wee the health of the people. The details of the measure most be watched at every turn, and they must give the rulers of the people to understand that they should resist to the death anything that was going to take from them the power of combination and of their trade unions, which bed been one of the gretteat and most powerful levers for good the workers had ever bad. (Applause). Sergeant James Washington stationed et Lymm, gave evidence of prisoner's arrest and as to the statement made by prisoner when arrested. DISEASED MEAT FOR SALE AT EARLESTOWN. CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY FINED.

An interesting case was heard at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Weduesdity, before Mr. S.R. I Armitage (presiding), Colouel J. D. Buckton and Mr. O. E. Palter, when the Earlestown Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society, Ltd., were charged with having exposed for sale in their chop in Earle-street, two hind quarters of beef which had been pronornmed diseased by the (inhume* Inspeotor.—Mr.G.Ellis(Wigan)prosecuted on behalf of the Newton-in•Makerfleld Urban District Connell, and Mr. Somers (Manchester) appeared for the Society. A plea of guilty was put in. Mr. Ellis stated that under the circumstance. in which the business of the Svclety was carried out they were bound.to rely on servants. In this case the offence had been committed by the head butcher. Although the offence was a serious one he had been instructed not to preen; the case. The nuisance inspector visited the Society's slaughterhouse on May 9th, and there saw • cow which was coughing. His suspicions being aroused he warned the head butcher. He inquired the time. of . . . .

the killing of the animal and was told it would take place that afternoon, lie again paid a •hit in the afternoon but seeing no preparations for killing he went away and called the following morning. The animal in the meantime however had been slaughtered and was put up for sale in the shop. There seemed to have been a determination on the part of the butcher who had ignored the warning not to cop sae the diseased meat for sale. Mr. Somers said he quite agreed that a serious offence had been committed and there ooght to beau risk in a caw, where it affected the food supply. This I was a case, however, in which to inflict a heavy penalty would be a great hardship on the Society on account of the may in which it was carried on. The weakness wee seen in the fact that the Society carried on a variety of trades altogether and the result was that the committee were not experienced in all the particular departments and so had to rely on their servant, to a large extent. This was an eaperienced butcher and he had been repeatedly warned to take precautiona when there was a suspicion of any dessased meat. Having relied upon this man and he having failed to do hie duty, they thought the matter so serious as to have no alternative but to discharge him. Nobody in authority saw this beset except the butcher sad he had failed to do his duty. Seeing that the Society must be punished under the circumstances be thought justice would be met by inflicting moderate penalty. The Bench lined the Society £5 in respect of each of Ike two pieces (flub in all).

div.head: IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
div.p: IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
THE PEERS, THE VETO, AND HOME RULE.

It will be seen, by the time the "Examiner' is in the hands of its readers, lif the will of the people is to be at last asserted or whether through bluff on one side and weakness on the other the constitu- encies are to be asked to repeat a verdict they have already thrice returned. The theatrical show and the empty farce which is being enacted in the House of Lords will then be over. As was expected we have had Lord Lansdowne's amendment duly moved, making as it did a complete mockery of the Government's proposals. Nothing could be more interesting than the part which the Irish question played in Tuesday evening's debate. Yet again for the thousandth time we heard the pitiful wailings of the Peers pronouncing their view that the country has not expressed itself on Home Rule. The Marquis of Londonderry even brought ballad poetry in to express his determined opposi- tion to any Home Rule settlement and in his characteristically superior fashion my Lord Curzon essayed to show that Home Rule was never heard of in the General Election of December last. Exhibitions of bovine intelligence and crass stupidity of this sort almost force one into hopelessness at their Lordships' capacity for anything out of Ascot or Monte Carlo. Surely these pillars of the State have weakened even worse than their harshest critics seriously contend if they seriously expect commonsense men to accept this kind of talk when the words of Lord Lansdowne himself at Portsmouth are still fresh in the mind of the English electorate. In the plainest terms possible the noble lord said if Mr. Asquith and his Party were returned then the electorate desired Home Rule to be granted. The words of this august person were borne by the press, Liberal and Unionist alike into every hamlet and town of the kingdom, and the return of the Liberal Government openly pledged that Home Ruin was the result. Have these people with coronets been bereft of memory or is it con- templated that there are no limits to bluff? On the point of the Lords desiring to sit upon and exceptionally consider a Home Rule Bill, Lord Morley rose to the top of his old form. Leaving passionate talk and declamation to the Curzons and the Mayos, Lord Morley challenged their lord- ships to deny that their House for over one hundred years had been the stronghold of those fierce partisans who had shown to Ireland the bitterest animosities of race and creed.

_ We suppose the Lords will be allowed to go on to the bitter end. The mutilated Bill will then be sent to the Commons when the Government will return it with an instruc- tion that all the material amendments have been rejected. Whether the Ministers share the impatier.ce felt by their supporters at this delay we do not of course know, but from the leading organs of the press and the reports of their several organisations they must needs know that the people are resolved to end the Peers' game. The Irish Unionist Peers we notice are pressing for a postponement of the Report Stage until after the King's visit to Ireland. As to that amazing proposal which could scarcely have come from men with a sense of the fitness of public things, all that need be remarked here is that it is not complimentary to the King. WILD ELECTION RUMOURS.

As to what turn high political events will take there is an astonishing diversity lof opinion in quarters all claiming inspiration of an authoritative and exclusive character. A London news- paper bids its readers prepare for a General Election in August—a few days back we were given July as the date. Sir Henry Lucy claim- ing high authority for his information ,as he did when he threatened grave calamities recently with regard to the Lord Chancellor and the magistracy) is quite con- fident that Mr. Asquith neither sought nor obtained guarantees for the success of the toil in which he and his supporters have been engaged for the last 19 months. The " Spectator " and the " Observer " are both frank in expressing their misgivings, from a Unionist point of view, at the prospect of a General Election and both these influential Tory papers put all their strength in last week's issue in the exhortation to the Peers to save their own House, and to pass the Veto Bill.

_ Fortunately within the next few days the air will be cleared of the rumours and counter rumours. For a day or two more we must " wait and see." But to the Irish Nationalist mind, the suggestion that the issue of the long struggle which has taxed the patience of the people is to be another election seems the wildest notion which the controversy has brought out.

"The Declaration 0 of London," Is now a main topic of controversy; and rightly so, since the interests of the British Empire, in the event of war, are deeply involved. It is of the greatest importance that the people of this country should grasp the whole meaning and effect of this International agreement; for when the people arrive at a conclusion upon a vital subject their will Is not to be gainsaid. In times of peace, and in matters that affect their well-being, the people have again and again do. Jared their unmistakable verdict. Nothing, for instance, is of more supreme con. / sequence than health, and in this particular the public have long ago decided that BEECHAM'S PILLS stand unrivalled among the means for securing and maintaining the bodily vigour of the community. This efficacLus medicine, which is now held In universal esteem, promotes a sound digestion, regu:a.e, the liver, bowels, and kidneys, and protects the very fountains and foundatiors of health from disorder and disease. This is not a "Declaration of London; alone. It is the opinion of the world at large —of Great Britain—of the Dominions overseas- -of America— A of Continental countries,and of the Far East. Wherever, indeed, Beecham's Pills have penetrated they have established themselves in the confidence of nations as possessing a value unequalled for general usefulness and fully justifying their reputation of being Worth a Guinea a Box.
